For the structured sorbent development, a sorbent-coated filter design was selected as the structured sorbent, which consists of: 1. Non-woven, electrically conductive substrate capable for direct joule heating 2. ECCOsorb-T1 DAC sorbent coated onto the electrically conductive nonwoven 3. Nonconductive nonwoven protective layer coated on top of the sorbent The sorbent coated onto the nonwoven filter provides high sorbent loading capacity. The electrically conductive nonwoven filter substrate can be Joule-heated to provide efficient utilization of available electricity for sorbent regeneration. A joint development agreement with a commercial filter manufacturing partner, a global leader in air filtration technology, was established to manufacture the structured sorbent. A key objective of the joint development effort was to determine if the existing filter manufacturing infrastructure can be utilized to scale Susteon’s structured sorbent filter concept, and that the manufactured structured sorbent filters can be used for DAC application. The commercial partner operated a pilot filter manufacturing line to produce 12 pleated filter panels coated with ECCOsorb-T1 and 10 flat filter laminate sheets for testing in Susteon’s bench-scale DAC unit. As part of this effort, Susteon scaled its sorbent synthesis process by 100-fold to produce over 50 kg of ECCOsorb-T1, which was the minimum sorbent quantity needed to operate the pilot filter manufacturing line. To demonstrate the filter concept as the structured sorbent, a 1 kg CO /day bench unit was designed and 2 fabricated. The bench-scale DAC unit included a DAC contactor capable of housing a full-size pleated filter Final Technical Report – Unlimited Rights Data 4 Susteon Inc. DE-FE0032254 with power feedthroughs and the control loop necessary for Joule-heated regeneration. Parametric testing with a single pleated filter was first completed to assess optimal operating conditions for the Joule-heated regeneration. Once completed, the fully assembled unit was tested with three pleated filters, which revealed sorbent instability due to non-uniform heating and localized hot spots in the pleats of the structured sorbent. A modified configuration consisting of stacked filter laminates was tested, which improved both sorbent capacity and stability but did not reach the target performance achieved in the screening reactor. Based on laboratory testing and characterization, the likely cause of the lower performance was due to sorbent active sites being occluded in the filter manufacturing process. Further optimization of filter manufacturing method is ongoing with commercial partner to prevent this issue in future development work. The key achievements from the structured sorbent development activity were demonstrating that existing filter industrial-scale processes can be used for manufacturing Susteon’s structured sorbent and completing a proof-of-concept demonstration of the commercially manufactured structured sorbent filters for CO 2 capture from air with direct, Joule-heated regeneration. A techno-economic assessment with sensitivity analysis was conducted on a 100,000 TPY facility with 85% operating capacity.
